MA342 overview

MA342 Topic Guide

Hausdorff Spaces

Separate points and use compact-to-Hausdorff rigidity.

Purpose

Test whether distinct points can be separated by disjoint open sets and exploit compact-Hausdorff consequences.Exam use: In 2025/26, Q2(c) assigns 6 marks to the definition and the lower-limit line, Q2(e) uses Hausdorffness in a 5-mark closedness proof, and Q4(a) asks why the Cantor set is compact Hausdorff.

Question plan

  1. Take arbitrary distinct x,y.
  2. Produce explicit neighbourhoods that are open in the named topology and prove they are disjoint.
  3. When compactness is also present, decide whether the target conclusion is closedness or a homeomorphism.
  4. Question interpretation: “Is X Hausdorff?” requires arbitrary distinct points, two named open neighbourhoods, and a disjointness check; a picture is not enough.

Definitions

X is Hausdorff if for x≠y there are disjoint open U,V with x∈U and y∈V. A continuous bijection from compact X to Hausdorff Y is a homeomorphism.Rapid recall: Hausdorff means distinct points have disjoint open neighbourhoods. Compact subsets of Hausdorff spaces are closed, and continuous maps from compact to Hausdorff spaces gain strong closedness properties.

Proof method

For a direct proof, fix x≠y and use the basis of the topology to construct disjoint neighbourhoods. For compact A⊆X and x∉A, separate x from every a∈A, take a finite subcover of A, and intersect only the finitely many neighbourhoods of x.Exam workflow: Fix arbitrary distinct points, choose topology-valid opens, verify membership and disjointness, then state the Hausdorff conclusion.

Worked simple example

R is Hausdorff: for x<y choose disjoint intervals around x and y, each with radius less than (y−x)/3.

Medium/hard paper-style synthesis

The lower-limit real line Rℓ is Hausdorff. Given x<y, take U=[x,y) and V=[y,y+1). Both are basic open sets, x∈U, y∈V, and U∩V=∅. Reversing the labels handles y<x, so every pair of distinct points has disjoint open neighbourhoods.

Graduated exam bridges

1. Foundation: Is an infinite cofinite space Hausdorff? Check: no: two nonempty opens always intersect, even though every singleton is closed.

2. Exam style [5 marks]: Prove a compact subspace A of Hausdorff X is closed. Check: separate each x∉A from all of A using a finite subcover.

Hard paper-style synthesis

The Cantor set C is Hausdorff because it is a subspace of standard R, and subspaces of Hausdorff spaces are Hausdorff. It is compact because it is closed in the compact interval [0,1]. Both claims require naming the inherited topology and the relevant hereditary theorem.

Practice question - lower-limit Hausdorffness [6 marks]

Inspired by: MA342 2025/26 Q2(c). Task. (a) Define what it means for a topological space to be Hausdorff. (b) Decide, with justification, whether the real line with the lower-limit topology is Hausdorff. [6 marks]

Demand diagnosis and fastest route: order arbitrary distinct points and use adjacent half-open basis intervals whose shared endpoint belongs only to the second interval.

Worked answer: A topological space X is Hausdorff if for every x≠y there exist disjoint open sets U,V with x∈U and y∈V. Let x<y in Rℓ. The basic-open sets U=[x,y) and V=[y,y+1) contain x and y respectively and are disjoint. If y<x, interchange the labels. Therefore Rℓ is Hausdorff.

Topic-specific trap: [x,y) and [y,y+1) work because the first interval excludes y; ordinary closed intervals would not be open in the lower-limit topology.

Mistakes

  • Finding neighbourhoods that are not disjoint.
  • Assuming T₁ automatically means Hausdorff.
  • Omitting continuity in the compact-Hausdorff theorem.
  • Recovery rule: T1 separates a point from another by one open set; it does not provide the pair of disjoint neighbourhoods required for Hausdorffness.

Checklist

  • I can state Hausdorff separation.
  • I can prove the lower-limit line is Hausdorff from its basis.
  • I can disprove it in an infinite cofinite topology.
  • I can write the compact-Hausdorff proof chain.
  • Final 60-second audit: Points are arbitrary and distinct, both neighbourhoods are open, containment and disjointness are proved, and theorem hypotheses are named.

Past-paper note

High confidence: Hausdorff definitions and consequences occur in all three papers from 2023/24 through 2025/26. The new paper directly tests lower-limit Hausdorffness in Q2(c), compact-subspace closedness in Q2(e), and the Cantor set’s Hausdorff property in Q4(a). Back to paper evidence.
